newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine peso tumbles after de facto devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Philippine peso tumbles after de facto devaluation.

text.p: The Philippine peso slumped on Monday after its de facto devaluation but an initial surge in the share market quickly fizzled out.

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, or central bank, launched a witch-hunt to find out if any local banks were involved in last week's repeated speculative attacks on the peso which resulted in the currency's 11.5 percent plunge to near four-year lows.
The peso touched a new low of 29.75 per dollar late in the morning but volume was extremely thin and traders were wary about doing any deals.
"The traders are just staring at their screens," one dealer said. "They don't want to be disturbed."
No one was quite sure what the peso's correct level should be, though many traders consider the current level, or slightly weaker, about right.
The peso has been cosseted for almost two years by the central bank which saw a stable currency as crucial if inflation was to be kept under control.
But by Friday, the Philippines became the second Asian country in as many weeks to succumb to currency speculators.
Manila's central bank admitted it could no longer afford to whittle away its foreign exchange reserves in a futile defence of the peso and at the end of last week finally surrendered to speculators.
On Monday, speculators switched their focus from Thailand and the Philippines to Malaysia where the ringgit dropped to a 16-month low. The Indonesian rupiah also came under attack.
Businessmen are now hoping that interest rates -- driven up to 2-1/2 year highs to defend the peso -- will now start to fall.
The initial response of the Philippine stock market was to surge again, but it quickly ran out of steam and by the close the main index had fallen slightly to 2,710.73 points.
"It looks like investors want to see stability first in the foreign exchange market before taking back positions," said Juanis Barredo, vice-president at Citisecurities Inc.
The central bank announced it had started to look into the accounts of onshore banks, especially those involved in large deals to see if any rules were broken.

"We'll have to impose sanctions on these banks (that exceeded their limits). We're calling up the banks, those who bought heavily and trying to find out what happened," central bank Governor Gabriel Singson said.
The central bank limits the amount of long or short dollar positions onshore banks may hold and makes it difficult to buy large amounts of dollars without underlying business justification.
Economists say the peso drop is certain to lead to higher inflation and will reduce economic growth this year.
Government officials claimed the impact would be slight though President Fidel Ramos at the weekend urged Filipinos to stay calm after the peso's tumble.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) immediately pledged to support Manila in what is its first chance to try out emerging funding rules introduced after the Mexico financial crisis which erupted at the end of 1994.

An IMF source in Washington told Reuters that accelerated procedures to offer the Philippines a support package of at least $600 million relied on rules under the IMF's so-called emergency financing mechanism.
